---
title: "Partial Differentiation and Gradients"
description: "An original worked mathematical lesson corresponding to MML §5.2."
---

**Reference:** *Mathematics for Machine Learning*, Chapter 5, §5.2. The teaching example and explanation here are original.

## Why we need this concept

A real predictor uses an intercept, distance and item count. The gradient collects how the loss changes when each parameter moves independently.

## Derive the structure

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}L=\begin{bmatrix}\partial L/\partial\beta_0\\\partial L/\partial\beta_1\\\partial L/\partial\beta_2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Check the shapes and conditions in this statement before applying it. The formula encodes the exact relationship to reason about, rather than replacing a derivation with a library call.

## Worked example

For one order with features x=(1,2,1), y=9, and beta=(3,2,1), prediction is 8. The squared loss gradient is 2(8-9)(1,2,1)=(-2,-4,-2). The negative gradient points toward local improvement.

## Interpretation and limitations

The gradient is a vector in parameter space, not input-feature space. Its components depend on feature scales; standardisation can improve optimisation conditioning.

## Challenge

Which coordinate of the gradient has the largest magnitude in the example, and why?
